items.title: Lenny's team tests OpenAI DevDay 2026: what's actually worth using
items.summary: A 24-minute walkthrough where Claire tries OpenAI's new DevDay features — Dots, Spaces, Sites, AI thumbnail picking, even a $97 vibe-coded game — and ranks what product people should try first.
items.why: A PM-filtered shortcut through 20+ announcements, so you know which new OpenAI capabilities are worth a real experiment this week.

cards.front: Dots (OpenAI)
cards.back: Proactive assistants that keep working on multi-step projects in the background, checking in with you rather than waiting for each prompt.

cards.front: Why watch a hands-on DevDay review instead of the recap page?
cards.back: Vendor recaps list features; hands-on reviews show which ones actually work and which are demo-ware — cheaper than testing all yourself.

quiz.q: What distinguishes OpenAI's 'dots' from a normal chatbot conversation?
options: They work proactively across a project over time instead of one prompt at a time
They run entirely on your own device with no network calls
They only generate images and video rather than text
They are a cheaper model tier with a smaller context window
quiz.why: Dots are framed as proactive assistants that keep progressing work across tasks, not single-turn responders.

items.title: GPT-6.1 Sol: near-flagship quality at a fifth of the price
items.summary: OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Sol, claiming close to Astra-level reasoning for coding, computer use and professional tasks at roughly 20% of Astra's API token prices. It's already generally available on Amazon Bedrock.
items.why: Price-per-quality drops reset what your agents can afford to do per request — and Bedrock availability means your stack can use it now.

cards.front: Why does a cheaper 'near-flagship' model change product decisions?
cards.back: Workloads you rejected on cost (per-item classification, retries, multi-step agents) become viable, so you can re-open shelved ideas.

cards.front: Input vs output tokens
cards.back: You pay separately for tokens sent in (prompt/context) and tokens generated out; long contexts and chatty outputs both drive cost.

quiz.q: GPT-6.1 Sol is pitched as 'near-Astra intelligence for a fifth of the price.' What does that most directly change for a product team?
options: High-volume or multi-step agent workloads become affordable at good quality
Model responses become deterministic and no longer need evaluation
Data no longer leaves your AWS region when you call the model
Context windows become unlimited so prompts need no trimming
quiz.why: Cost per token is the constraint on frequent, multi-call agent work; quality-per-dollar gains unlock those use cases, not determinism or residency.

items.title: Eight things you can build when the model is nearly free (Jev demos)
items.summary: John Lindquist demos eight uses of Jev, an extremely fast and cheap model: live voice classification, deduplication, agent routing and more — arguing ultra-low cost makes previously impractical patterns sensible.
items.why: Concrete patterns for cheap-model plumbing (routing, classification, dedup) — the unglamorous parts of production agents you're learning to build.

items.title: OpenAI's 'dots': proactive assistants that keep working
items.summary: OpenAI introduced dots, assistants designed to make progress on long-running projects and routine tasks on their own while still surfacing checkpoints so the user stays in control.
items.why: This is the industry moving from chat to background agents — the same UX questions (trust, checkpoints, undo) you face in your own agent features.

items.title: Claude Code v2.1.285: kill switch for WebFetch, desktop handoff, plugin config
items.summary: New release adds an environment variable to disable the WebFetch tool, a `claude --desktop` command to open the current directory or a resumed session in the desktop app, and a command to inspect plugin configuration.
items.why: Useful day-to-day: disabling WebFetch tightens what Claude can pull from the web, and --desktop moves a session between interfaces.

items.title: Building a cited, natural-language document assistant on Bedrock Knowledge Bases
items.summary: AWS walks through a claims-question assistant: ingest documents from S3, retrieve with an agentic streaming API, handle follow-up turns, filter by metadata, and use contextual grounding guardrails to curb made-up answers.
items.why: A blueprint for retrieval-over-your-documents on the exact AWS stack your production agents already run on, including grounding guardrails.

items.title: Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances: multi-agent workflows with shared state
items.summary: AWS added long-running runtime instances where several agents share one GPU machine, a persistent filesystem and multi-day sessions, demonstrated with a three-agent pipeline that hands work between agents to finish a music track.
items.why: Your agents on Lambda are short-lived; this shows AWS's answer for multi-agent work that needs hours, shared files and handoffs.

items.title: The full DevDay 2026 firehose, digested
items.summary: An AI-news roundup of everything OpenAI shipped: GPT-6.1 Sol, an Ultrafast tier, Decisions and Agents APIs, Spaces, a marketplace, and the claim of 1.2 billion weekly ChatGPT users.
items.why: Skim to see the platform shift: OpenAI is selling agent infrastructure and distribution, not just models — relevant to your roadmap bets.

items.title: Claude models get in-region inference in Seoul, Singapore and India
items.summary: Bedrock now processes Claude Opus 5 and Sonnet 5 requests entirely within Seoul, Sonnet 5 in Singapore, and offers India in-country inference, aimed at local data-processing requirements.
items.why: If a market ever asks where your agent's data is processed, this is the Bedrock lever that answers it without changing models.

items.title: Every Lenny & Friends Summit talk is now free to watch
items.summary: Lenny released full video of all Summit talks plus his own notes on the biggest themes from the day — product craft, AI-era team shapes, and career advice from the speakers.
items.why: A concentrated dose of the thinkers you already follow; pick one talk per walk instead of hunting for podcast episodes.

items.title: Claude Sonnet 5.5: faster, cheaper, beats Sonnet 5 across benchmarks
items.summary: Anthropic shipped Sonnet 5.5 at the same list price as Sonnet 5 but roughly 30% faster and up to 30% cheaper per task, with benchmark wins across the board and a 1M-token context.
items.why: Sonnet is your everyday workhorse in Claude Code; switching gets you speed and cost wins with no quality tradeoff.

cards.front: Claude Sonnet 5.5
cards.back: Anthropic's mid-tier model, released Sep 2026: ~30% faster and up to 30% cheaper per task than Sonnet 5, same list price, 1M-token context.

cards.front: Why does a 'mid-tier' model matter if Opus exists?
cards.back: Sonnet handles most focused coding and knowledge work at a fraction of Opus's cost and latency — better economics for agents that run many steps.

quiz.q: What is the main improvement Anthropic claims for Claude Sonnet 5.5 over Sonnet 5?
options: Similar price, but faster and lower cost per task with better benchmarks
Higher price, justified by a much larger training dataset
Same speed, but a new dedicated image-generation capability
Lower benchmarks, offset by a far cheaper per-token price
quiz.why: Anthropic priced it the same as Sonnet 5 while claiming ~30% faster, up to 30% cheaper per task, and better scores across benchmarks.

items.title: Claude Code v2.1.284 adds Sonnet 5.5 and a smarter permission prompt
items.summary: The new release makes Sonnet 5.5 the default Sonnet model (1M context, $2/$10 per million tokens) and adds a "Yes, but ask again next time" option when Claude wants to read a file outside your working directory.
items.why: You'll see both changes today: a cheaper default model and finer-grained control over what Claude Code is allowed to read.

cards.front: What does "Yes, but ask again next time" do in Claude Code?
cards.back: Approves one single action (e.g. reading a file outside your project folder) without granting a standing permission for future ones.

cards.front: Why does Claude Code ask before reading outside the working directory?
cards.back: Files outside your project aren't part of the agreed scope; the prompt prevents accidental exposure of unrelated or sensitive files.

quiz.q: In Claude Code, choosing "Yes, but ask again next time" for an out-of-directory read means:
options: Only this one read is allowed; future ones still prompt
All reads in that folder are allowed for the session
The read is queued until you end the session
Claude reads the file but cannot edit anything after
quiz.why: It's a one-time approval, keeping the permission prompt active for later reads instead of granting a blanket allow.

items.title: Anthropic's Claude Code lead on what's coming next
items.summary: An interview with Thariq Shihipar covering the Opus/Sonnet 5.5 launch and Claude Code's newer surfaces — Mods, Plugins, Projects and Tag — plus how the team decides what to ship as models improve.
items.why: Hearing the product thinking behind your daily tool tells you which features to adopt and where the workflow is heading.

items.title: Sonnet 5.5 lands on Amazon Bedrock
items.summary: AWS made Claude Sonnet 5.5 available on Bedrock and the Claude Platform, with guidance on when to route work to Sonnet rather than Opus based on cost per task and latency.
items.why: Your production agents run on Bedrock — this is the concrete path to cutting their cost and latency without a rewrite.

items.title: Grok 4.7 joins Amazon Bedrock with 500K context
items.summary: xAI's Grok 4.7 is now callable through Bedrock's Converse and Chat Completions APIs, offering a 500K-token window and four selectable reasoning-effort levels aimed at coding and long-running agents.
items.why: Useful context on Bedrock's growing model menu: you can swap models behind the same API and tune reasoning effort per task.

items.title: A reference pattern for agents that extract and verify data from documents
items.summary: AWS walks through a contract-intelligence build on Bedrock AgentCore: agents pull structured fields out of contracts, a second pass verifies them, and an analytics layer answers portfolio-wide questions that plain RAG chat can't.
items.why: Shows why retrieval chat fails on "across all documents" questions, and a production-shaped alternative on your own stack.

items.title: OpenAI publishes early guidelines for AI training "safety cases"
items.summary: OpenAI outlines how it plans to argue that a frontier training run is safe: technical safeguards, operational practices, and procedures for investigating misalignment incidents when they appear.
items.why: Safety-case language is starting to appear in enterprise AI procurement and risk reviews you may be asked to fill out.

items.title: AMD buys World Labs for $8.2B as spatial AI heats up
items.summary: AMD's acquisition of World Labs, alongside the Atlas model tackling sparse 3D reconstruction, signals serious money moving into world models and spatial AI for robotics and design tooling.
items.why: Useful trend radar: the frontier is widening beyond text models into spatial understanding, which will reshape some product categories.

items.title: Lenny's How I AI roundup: Opus 5.5 vs GPT-6, and Jev for beginners
items.summary: Weekly roundup from Lenny's How I AI network: a beginner guide to Jev, a creator explaining why Opus 5.5 pulled them back from a rival model, and a head-to-head Opus 5.5 vs GPT-6 benchmark.
items.why: Your main source for how PMs actually pick and switch models; frontier comparisons directly affect which model you default to in Claude Code.

cards.front: Why do practitioners re-benchmark models after each release?
cards.back: Frontier models leapfrog each other; a model that lost on your task six months ago may now win, so default choices should be re-tested, not assumed.

cards.front: What is a 'head-to-head bench' in these roundups?
cards.back: Running the same real tasks through two models and comparing output quality, speed and cost — more useful for PMs than public leaderboard scores.

quiz.q: Why is a self-run head-to-head test on your own tasks usually more useful than a public leaderboard score?
options: It reflects your actual prompts, data and quality bar, which leaderboards don't capture
It uses more test cases than the benchmarks vendors publish
It measures the model's parameter count more accurately than vendors do
It removes the effect of temperature settings on the results
quiz.why: Leaderboards average over generic tasks; relevance to your workflow is what decides which model to default to.

items.title: Simon Willison's annotated review of what changed in LLMs during 2026
items.summary: Conference keynote walking chronologically through the year's model releases, agent trends and shifts in how people build with LLMs, with annotated slides and notes rather than hype.
items.why: The fastest single catch-up on the model landscape — ideal for filling gaps before you argue for a model or agent choice at work.

cards.front: Why track LLM releases chronologically rather than by vendor?
cards.back: It shows how capabilities (long context, agentic tool use, cheap small models) diffused across all labs, so you can judge trends instead of marketing claims.

cards.front: What is an 'agentic' model in 2026 terms?
cards.back: A model trained and tuned to plan, call tools repeatedly and work over long sessions, not just answer a single prompt.

quiz.q: What distinguishes an 'agentic' model from a standard chat model?
options: It is optimised for multi-step planning and repeated tool calls over a task
It is trained on more languages so it answers in the user's locale
It stores past chats permanently so it never needs context re-sent
It runs on the client device instead of in the provider's cloud
quiz.why: Agentic tuning targets long-horizon tool use and planning, which is why such models power coding agents.

items.title: Using Jev to get typed, structured outputs as a cheap classification layer
items.summary: A 26-minute walkthrough of Jev, which returns type-safe structured values instead of free text — presented as a fast, cheap classification step inside pipelines, with three shipped example projects.
items.why: Structured output instead of parsing text is the key pattern for reliable production agents — exactly what your Lambda+Bedrock services need.

items.title: Agent-driven monitoring with Amazon Nova Act and Bedrock AgentCore
items.summary: AWS shows an architecture where an agent performs user-journey checks instead of brittle scripted UI tests, using Nova Act plus Bedrock AgentCore, including patterns for resilience and a sample implementation.
items.why: Runs on your exact stack (Bedrock) and shows a production agent pattern plus AgentCore, the managed runtime you may end up owning.

items.title: An AI agent auto-replied 'I'm here!' when its owner wasn't — a failure worth studying
items.summary: A quoted transcript where a personal AI assistant admits its automatic reply misled a real person during a pickup, causing a negative rating — a concrete example of autonomous agents acting without confirmation.
items.why: A vivid, shareable illustration of why agents acting on your behalf need human confirmation gates before irreversible, real-world actions.

items.title: S3 storage prices haven't dropped in a decade
items.summary: Simon Willison notes that Amazon S3's per-gigabyte price has stayed flat for around ten years despite falling hardware costs, prompting discussion of cloud storage economics and competitors.
items.why: Cheap useful context on cloud cost assumptions when you plan AI features that store logs, documents or model artefacts on AWS.

items.title: Molly Graham on burnout, grief, and delegating work to AI instead of people
items.summary: Molly Graham updates her classic "give away your Legos" career advice for the AI era, discussing industry-wide grief, loneliness and burnout, and why handing work to an agent feels nothing like handing it to a teammate.
items.why: You delegate to Claude Code daily; this reframes what that does to your role, your team's morale and your own career growth.

cards.front: "Give away your Legos" (Molly Graham)
cards.back: As a company scales, you must hand off work you love to others; the discomfort is normal and necessary for growth.

cards.front: Why is delegating to an AI agent different from delegating to a person?
cards.back: No one grows on the receiving end — you lose the mentoring, trust-building and team capacity that human handoffs create, while keeping the loss of the work itself.

quiz.q: What is the core point of Molly Graham's "give away your Legos" advice?
options: Handing off work you enjoy is painful but necessary as the org scales
Keeping ownership of your best projects protects your career growth
Delegating only low-value tasks keeps your team motivated over time
Rebuilding your role from scratch each year prevents professional burnout
quiz.why: The metaphor is about the discomfort of surrendering work you love so a growing company can scale.

items.title: Community Wisdom: AI doomerism, faster discovery in big orgs, and checking engineers' answers as a new PM
items.summary: Reader Q&A roundup from Lenny's community covering how to handle AI anxiety, speeding up product discovery inside large organizations, sanity-checking engineering estimates without a technical background, and where analytics actually pays off.
items.why: The thread on verifying engineering answers as a non-technical PM maps directly onto your goal of building technical confidence.

items.title: Stripe buys OpenRouter for $7B: why model routing became valuable
items.summary: A podcast with OpenRouter's founder on how the model landscape exploded from two frontier labs to dozens, and why a neutral router that lets apps swap between models became a $7B acquisition for Stripe.
items.why: You pick models for agents; routing layers let you swap providers without rewrites, and Stripe's bet signals where AI infrastructure value is concentrating.

cards.front: What is an LLM router (e.g. OpenRouter)?
cards.back: A service sitting between your app and many model providers, exposing one API so you can switch or fall back between models without changing code.

cards.front: Why does multi-model routing matter for production agents?
cards.back: It reduces vendor lock-in, enables cost/quality tradeoffs per task, and provides failover when one provider is slow or down.

quiz.q: What does a service like OpenRouter primarily provide?
options: One API that routes requests across many model providers
A fine-tuning service that customises open-weight models
A vector database for storing document embeddings
A framework for orchestrating multi-step agent workflows
quiz.why: OpenRouter is an aggregation/routing layer giving a single interface to dozens of models, not a training, storage, or orchestration tool.

items.title: Five techniques for QA-ing LLM output in production on Bedrock
items.summary: An AWS write-up on keeping LLM answers reliable at scale: orchestrating pipelines adaptively, failing over across accounts and models, evaluating responses while they stream, combining several evaluation signals, and verifying numerical accuracy.
items.why: Your agents run on Bedrock; these are concrete, reusable patterns for evaluation and failover you can put on a roadmap.

cards.front: Multi-model failover
cards.back: Routing a request to a backup model (or account/region) when the primary is rate-limited, erroring, or too slow — key for production reliability.

cards.front: Streaming evaluation
cards.back: Checking an LLM's output for errors as tokens are generated, so bad answers can be caught or stopped before the user sees the whole response.

quiz.q: Why would an AI team add cross-account, multi-model failover to a Bedrock service?
options: To keep serving users when the primary model hits limits or errors
To lower token costs by compressing prompts before sending them
To fine-tune the model on customer data without leaving the account
To cache identical prompts so repeat answers return instantly
quiz.why: Failover is a reliability pattern: a backup model/account takes over when the primary is throttled or failing. The others are cost or training techniques.

items.title: Simon Willison: coding agents make engineering harder, not easier
items.summary: A short but pointed note arguing that coding agents raise the ceiling of what's possible while demanding more discipline and knowledge from the person driving them — not less.
items.why: A useful counterweight when planning AI-assisted delivery: expect review, testing and judgement costs to rise, not vanish.

items.title: Meta's Muse gives every user their own cloud Linux machine
items.summary: Commentary on Meta's new Muse product: each user gets a persistent Linux virtual machine in Meta's cloud, wrapped in consumer-grade easy installation — a notable example of hiding heavy infrastructure behind simple packaging.
items.why: Good product lesson: the differentiator isn't the VM, it's making serious compute feel like installing an app.

items.title: Zapier's AI fluency rubric: how every employee gets graded on AI use
items.summary: Zapier's CEO shares the internal rubric rating staff from 'unacceptable' to 'transformative' on AI use, plus concrete behaviours PMs show at each level: delegating whole workflows, building internal tools, and rewiring team process around agents.
items.why: It gives you a concrete yardstick for your own AI fluency and language to push your team from 'uses chat' to 'redesigns workflows'.

cards.front: What is an 'AI fluency rubric'?
cards.back: A company-wide scale rating how deeply an employee uses AI — from avoiding it, to occasional chat use, to delegating full workflows and building tools that change how the team works.

cards.front: What separates 'transformative' AI use from 'adequate' use?
cards.back: Adequate = faster at existing tasks. Transformative = rebuilding the workflow itself, e.g. agents doing multi-step work and internally built tools others adopt.

quiz.q: In Zapier's AI fluency framing, what best distinguishes a top-rated ('transformative') employee?
options: They redesign workflows so agents handle whole multi-step jobs others adopt
They use an AI assistant daily to draft documents and summarise meetings
They have tried every major frontier model and can compare their strengths
They can write detailed prompts with examples, roles and output formats
quiz.why: The rubric rewards changing how work happens, not personal speed-ups or tool familiarity.

items.title: Multi-account AI agents on Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with MCP
items.summary: AWS walks through an architecture where a central account runs an agent that reaches data in other teams' AWS accounts, each exposing its data as an MCP server, with cross-account auth and per-user permissions via AgentCore Gateway.
items.why: This is your stack: Bedrock plus agents. It shows the standard pattern for letting one agent safely query data owned by other teams.

cards.front: MCP (Model Context Protocol)
cards.back: An open standard letting an AI agent connect to external tools and data sources through a consistent interface, so each system exposes its capabilities as an 'MCP server'.

cards.front: What does Bedrock AgentCore Gateway do?
cards.back: It sits between an agent and many tool/data endpoints, handling discovery, authentication and fine-grained authorization — including across separate AWS accounts.

quiz.q: Why expose each team's data as an MCP server instead of copying it into the agent's account?
options: Data stays owned and governed by its team while the agent queries it through one interface
MCP servers compress data so the model can fit more of it in context
It removes the need for authentication because MCP traffic is internal to AWS
It lets the agent run without a foundation model when answering data questions
quiz.why: The pattern's point is federated access with per-account ownership and fine-grained authorization, not compression or skipping auth.

items.summary: Runway's world model generates video and audio on the fly, using persistent context plus timed action prompts so users can direct an interactive scene as it plays rather than rendering a fixed clip.
items.why: A glimpse of prompting as continuous steering rather than one-shot requests — a UX pattern likely to spread to agent products.

items.title: Meta Connect 2026: Muse smart glasses and new voice/video AI

items.title: Advanced evals: finding the AI failures you don't know about
items.summary: Lenny's newsletter walks through error discovery — systematically surfacing hidden failure modes in an AI product before writing eval criteria, so your metrics measure real problems instead of imagined ones.
items.why: You ship agents; evals are the PM skill that separates demo-grade from production-grade. Error discovery is the step most teams skip.

cards.front: Error discovery (in AI evals)
cards.back: Reading real outputs/traces to find actual failure modes first, then turning those into eval criteria — instead of guessing metrics up front.

cards.front: Why not start with a metric?
cards.back: Predefined metrics miss failure modes you haven't imagined; you optimize for what you measured, not what breaks.

cards.front: Who should do error discovery?
cards.back: A domain expert or PM who can judge 'good' — it's judgment work, not just engineering.

quiz.q: According to the eval workflow, what should come first?
options: Pick a scoring metric and benchmark
Look at real outputs to discover failure modes
Fine-tune the model
Add more tools to the agent
quiz.why: Error discovery precedes criteria: you can only measure failures you've actually found.

weekly.headline: Frontier week: Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 land with 40-50% price cuts, Stripe pays $7B for a model router, and evals become the PM skill to own.
weekly.script:
Big week. Start with the models: Anthropic's Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol and Luna shipped within about a day of each other, Grok 4.7 too, and frontier prices were cut roughly forty to fifty percent. Two takeaways for you. First, your cost assumptions for your Bedrock agents are now wrong in your favour, so it's worth re-running the per-million-token math before your next roadmap conversation. Second, Opus 5.5 is already live on Bedrock, so testing it is a config change, not a project. Lenny even ran blind head-to-head tests and found the winner depends on the task, which is a good habit to steal: judge by your own tasks, not benchmark charts.

Second story: Stripe bought OpenRouter for seven billion dollars. OpenRouter is a routing layer that sits between your app and dozens of models, so you can swap providers without rewriting anything. When a payments giant pays that much for a switchboard, it's telling you that optionality between models is where infrastructure value is concentrating, and that locking yourself to one provider is now a real product risk.

Third: Lenny's piece on advanced evals. The key idea is error discovery. Before you write any scoring criteria, go hunting through real outputs for failure modes you didn't know existed, otherwise your metrics measure imaginary problems. That's the step most teams skip, and it's the line between demo-grade and production-grade.

Fourth, straight onto your stack: AWS published a pattern where one central agent reaches data owned by other teams' AWS accounts, with each team exposing its data as an MCP server and AgentCore Gateway handling cross-account auth and per-user permissions. That's the answer to "how does our agent query their data safely."

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of putting a model router in front of your AI product?
options: You can switch or fall back between providers without rewriting the application
You get a cheaper price per token than calling the provider's API directly
You remove the need to run your own evaluations on each model version
You keep the conversation history so the model no longer has to be re-sent
quiz.why: A router is a neutral interface across many models, so swapping providers becomes configuration rather than a rewrite. It doesn't replace evals, doesn't inherently discount tokens, and doesn't change the stateless nature of models.

A benchmark score that can be compared against published model leaderboards
A scoring rubric derived from the product requirements document
A fallback chain of models to use when the primary model is unavailable
quiz.why: Error discovery comes first: you surface the failures you didn't know about, then write eval criteria against them, so your metrics measure real problems rather than assumed ones.

quiz.q: In the AWS multi-account agent pattern, what job does AgentCore Gateway do?

Copies each team's data into the central account so the agent can query it
Fine-tunes a separate model per account to specialise on that team's data
Caches tool results across accounts to reduce per-token inference costs

weekly.headline: A frontier release week (Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Sol and Luna) plus a price war — and evals become the PM skill that matters
weekly.script:
Big week. Two things collided: new frontier models, and a fresh push on how we actually judge them.

Start with evals. Lenny's newsletter published a piece on advanced evals, and the key idea is error discovery: before you write a single scoring criterion, you go hunting for the failure modes you don't know your product has. Most teams invert this — they invent metrics first and end up measuring imaginary problems. For you, shipping agents, this is the line between a demo that impresses and something that survives real users.

Second, Simon Willison rounded up a chaotic release week. Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol and Luna landed within a day of each other, Grok 4.7 alongside them, and frontier prices dropped roughly forty to fifty percent. That means your cost assumptions for your Bedrock agents are stale. Re-run the math this week; things you priced out as too expensive may now be affordable.

Third, and conveniently: Opus 5.5 is already live on Amazon Bedrock. That's your exact stack — Lambda plus Bedrock — so testing it in a production agent is a config change, not a migration.

Fourth, Lenny ran blind head-to-head tests of Opus 5.5 versus GPT-6 Sol across six task types: writing, frontend prototypes, long-running agentic tasks, SVGs, coding and video editing. The lesson isn't which model won; it's the method. Pick models per task from your own blind tests, not from benchmark press releases.

Fifth, AWS published a guide to evaluating skill-equipped agents using Strands Evals with Bedrock AgentCore. It measures whether your agent picked the right skill and followed instructions — not just whether the answer sounded fluent. That's the native tooling twin of Lenny's evals piece.

One bonus: Warp's CEO described an AI factory turning Slack and Linear tickets into two thousand pull requests a month. Worth stealing the operating model for Bitbucket.
